stage.name: Main stage
stage.description: A fictional annual conference of the Halcyon blockchain ecosystem: its core developers, the projects building on it, and the institutions adopting it.

lines: S1
Good morning everyone and welcome to day one of Meridian Summit. Please find your seats, we are about to get started.
S1
A quick reminder that the wifi password is on the back of your badge, and coffee is served in the foyer at ten fifty.
S1
To open the main stage, please welcome the co-founder of Halcyon Labs, Mira Voss.
S2
Thank you Dan. Hello Meridian. It is good to be back in this room.
S2
I want to use these twenty minutes to tell you where Halcyon is going over the next two years, and I am going to start with the thing most of you came to hear.
S2
Today we are announcing that the Lattice upgrade goes live on mainnet on March the third. That date is locked.
S2

Lattice replaces our execution scheduler, and on the public testnet over the last ninety days it has sustained eighty five thousand transactions per second with a median confirmation of four hundred milliseconds.
S2
For comparison, mainnet today peaks at around eleven thousand. So this is close to an eight times improvement on the same hardware.
S2
The second thing. Fees. After Lattice, the median fee for a simple transfer drops below a hundredth of a cent. We think that makes fees a rounding error for consumer applications.
S2
Now some numbers on where the network is today. Halcyon passed four point two million daily active addresses in October, up from one point six million a year ago.
S2
And developers. We counted three thousand one hundred monthly active developers on Halcyon last month, which is the highest it has ever been.
S2
I also want to be honest about what went wrong. The outage in June lasted five hours and it was our fault. A bug in the gossip layer that our own test suite should have caught.
S2
Since then we have funded two independent validator clients, because no network should depend on one codebase. Ironwood is the first, and Tomas will talk about it later this morning.
S2
Our target is that by the end of next year no single client runs more than half of the stake.
S2
One more announcement. Halcyon Labs is partnering with Kestrel Bank to settle Kestrel's tokenised deposits on Halcyon, starting with a pilot in the second quarter.
S2
Kestrel is a regulated bank with forty billion dollars in deposits. This is not a marketing partnership. They are putting real balances on chain.
S2
Let me say something about where I think this industry is. My view is that the scaling debate is over. Blockspace is going to be abundant on every serious chain within two years.
S2
What will be scarce is distribution. The chains that win will be the ones wallets and banks already integrate, not the ones with the best benchmark.
S2
And I think most layer twos that exist today will not exist in three years, because their only product was cheaper blockspace.
S2
So that is the plan. Lattice on March the third. Fees near zero. Two more clients. And real banks on chain.
S2
On the roadmap after that, we plan to ship native account abstraction in the second half of next year, so a user never has to see a seed phrase.
S2
We are also committing fifty million dollars from the Halcyon ecosystem fund to teams building consumer payments. Applications open next week.
S2
I will stop there. Thank you all for building on Halcyon. Enjoy the summit.
S1
Mira Voss, everybody. Thank you Mira.
S1
Next up on the main stage we have a panel, Stablecoins after the yield era. Please welcome Priya Raman of Tessel, Jonas Weller of Kestrel Bank, and your moderator Elena Park from Fathom Research.
S3
Thanks Dan. I'm Elena Park, I cover stablecoins at Fathom Research. Let's get straight into it. Priya, Tessel issues the largest stablecoin on Halcyon. What changed this year?
S4
Thanks Elena. The big change is that the yield went away. When rates fell, the easy business of sitting on treasury bills and keeping the interest got a lot smaller.
S4
Tessel's reserve income is down about forty percent year on year, even though our supply grew. Our circulating supply is nine billion dollars today, up from six billion in January.
S4
So we have had to become a payments company. Sixty percent of our transfer volume now is merchant settlement and payroll, not trading.
S3
Jonas, you are the bank on this stage. Why would a bank issue deposits on a public chain at all?
S5
It is a fair question, Elena. Honestly, two years ago we would not have. What changed is that our corporate clients started asking for settlement on weekends.
S5
Kestrel will launch its tokenised deposit pilot in the second quarter with twelve corporate clients, and we expect to move about two billion dollars a month through it by the end of the year.
S5
I should be clear that a tokenised deposit is not a stablecoin. It is a claim on the bank, it is insured, and it pays interest. I think that is what most businesses will actually want to hold.
S4
I disagree with Jonas there. A deposit token only works between clients of the same bank. A stablecoin works between everyone. Open networks beat closed ones, they always have.
S5
Perhaps. But I would say regulators will not let non-banks hold nine billion dollars of other people's money without bank-like rules for much longer.
S3
Let's talk about that. Priya, do you expect to need a banking licence?
S4
We have applied for one. Tessel filed for a national trust charter in September, and we expect a decision in the first half of next year.
S4
And we are going to start sharing reserve income with holders. From January, Tessel will pass through half of its reserve yield to wallets that hold more than thirty days.
S3
That is news. Jonas, does that worry you?
S5
A little, yes. If stablecoins pay yield, they compete directly with deposits. My prediction is that within three years the difference between the two will be a legal detail the customer never sees.
S3
Last question for both of you. One number that will surprise this room a year from now?
S4
Stablecoin supply on Halcyon passes fifty billion dollars. It is at fourteen billion today.
S5
More than half of Kestrel's cross-border corporate payments will settle on chain.
S3
Priya Raman, Jonas Weller, thank you both.
S1
Thank you to our panel. We are going to take a short break now. Coffee is in the foyer, and we will be back on the main stage at five past eleven.
S1
A reminder that the workshop rooms are on the second floor, and lunch vouchers are at the registration desk.

Halcyon: the next two years.headline: Halcyon's Lattice upgrade goes live on mainnet on March 3, alongside a settlement pilot with Kestrel Bank.
Halcyon: the next two years.overview: Mira Voss set out Halcyon's plan for the next two years around four commitments: the Lattice upgrade on a fixed date, fees close to zero, more than one validator client, and regulated banks settling on chain. She acknowledged that June's five-hour outage was the team's own fault and presented client diversity as the answer to it. She closed with a view of the industry: blockspace is about to be abundant everywhere, so distribution through wallets and banks, not benchmarks, will decide which chains last.
key_points: Lattice replaces Halcyon's execution scheduler and ships to mainnet on March 3; Voss called the date locked.
On testnet Lattice held 85,000 transactions per second for 90 days, against a mainnet peak of about 11,000 today.
Halcyon Labs has funded two independent validator clients after June's outage and wants no client above half of stake by the end of next year.
Kestrel Bank will settle tokenised deposits on Halcyon, starting with a pilot in the second quarter.
Voss argued the scaling debate is over and that most of today's layer twos will be gone within three years.

Stablecoins after the yield era.overview: Elena Park pressed a stablecoin issuer and a bank on what is left of the business now that reserve income has fallen. Priya Raman said Tessel has turned into a payments company and will start passing yield to holders; Jonas Weller said Kestrel's corporate clients pushed it on chain by asking for weekend settlement. They disagreed on the end state: Weller expects businesses to prefer insured, interest-paying deposit tokens, while Raman argued that open stablecoins beat instruments that only work inside one bank. Both expect the two to converge under bank-like regulation.

Raman countered that a deposit token only works between clients of the same bank, and open networks win.
Weller predicted that within three years the difference will be a legal detail customers never see.
